text: Borrowed loosely from monetary economics, the equation of exchange is a rough mental model for how a token's required value relates to its usage: M times V equals P times Q — supply, times velocity, equals price times quantity of transactions.

Rearranged, token value needed equals P times Q, divided by V. If a protocol needs 100 million dollars a year in transaction value, and each token changes hands 10 times a year, the market only needs 10 million dollars worth of the token in circulation to support that — not 100 million.

That's why high velocity is a problem, not a feature, for a utility token's price. Take a protocol processing 50 million dollars a year in volume: at low velocity of 2, the required token market value is 25 million. At high velocity of 20, it's only 2.5 million. Same usage, radically different implied value.

This is exactly why staking lockups, vesting, and utility functions that require holding rather than instantly passing through — governance weight, fee discounts tied to a holding period — all work to reduce velocity and support price, independent of usage growth.

Tying the chapter together: every period, circulating supply changes based on inflows like emissions and vesting unlocks, and outflows like burns and new staking lockups. One quarter might see 3 million in emissions, 2 million in vesting unlocks, minus 1.5 million burned and 2.5 million newly locked — a net 1 million increase in liquid supply.

A model you could build in a spreadsheet lists every inflow and outflow as a function of time, nets it period by period, then stress-tests it against demand: what usage growth would be needed to absorb that net new liquid supply without price declining? That question closes out Chapter 5. Next: on-chain governance mechanics, and how voting and delegation actually work.
